text: 5-year-old boy. The patient is presented by his mother for a well-child visit. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, is currently up to date on all vaccines, and is meeting all developmental milestones. His mother reports that he has been generally doing well with no concerns. No family history of cardiovascular disease. The boy does not take any medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since this is an incidental finding of hypertension in a young child, I need to rule out renal causes. Does the patient have any history of urinary tract infections, abnormal urine color, or decreased urine output?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is High blood pressure on the right upper extremity.

speaker: Doctor
text: Let me clarify that last point; did you mean his blood pressure is high in the right arm, or is it elevated in all limbs? Also, is his blood pressure higher in his arms compared to his legs?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Born full term with an uneventful neonatal period. Social history: Patient attends kindergarten. Lives with parents and one younger sibling. No exposure to tobacco smoke.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is there a difference in blood pressure between his arms and legs, or are pulses weak or delayed in his lower extremities compared to his upper extremities? REQUEST TEST: Echocardiogram

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Blood_Pressure_Differential: Upper_Extremities: 150/80 mm Hg (Right), Compared to lower values in lower extremities; Echocardiogram: Narrowing of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery with a gradient, consistent with coarctation. Left ventricular function is normal.

speaker: Doctor
text: The blood pressure differential and echocardiogram findings confirm the diagnosis. DIAGNOSIS READY: Coarctation of the aorta
